transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-25
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Ella Rodriguez (Cloudline Head of ML), Marcus Lee (Cloudline Infra), Sophie Wang (CTO)

Summary (auto): discuss POC scope, harness integration, key metrics and timeline.

[00:00] Alex Morgan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. umm quick intro from our side, I'm Alex, AE on the account, and Priya will run the technical bits.
[00:18] Ella Rodriguez: Hi all, Ella here. We wanted to focus this call on benchmark planning and how we can plug our scripts into your harness. Sophie and Marcus are on to help with infra and approval.
[00:30] Priya Nair: Great, thanks. Quick ask before we jump in — can you confirm the core success criteria for this pilot? Latency, throughput, and any cost targets?
[00:45] Sophie Wang: Right, from product we care about latency p95 under 300ms for non-streaming text-generation on our 1k token average prompts, and for streaming flows we want stable per-token latency under ~30ms ideally. Throughput target is around 100-150 rps for our production route. Cost is secondary in the POC but we want ballpark numbers.
[01:10] Alex Morgan: That's helpful. We'll aim to validate p95 < 300ms non-streaming and then measure streaming per-token latency separately. For throughput, we'll plan sustained runs at 120 rps and also peak bursts to 250.
[01:30] Marcus Lee: One nuance — some calls are multi-turn with KV cache reuse. How do you want us to model cache hits vs cold starts?
[01:45] Priya Nair: Good question. For the harness we support scripted sessions that can emulate multi-turns and cache behavior. Ideally we provide two workloads: 1) cold-start single-turn distribution, 2) multi-turn sessions with KV reuse rate settable (e.g., 70% cache hit). Can you give us typical session length?
[02:10] Ella Rodriguez: Average session is 3.5 turns, up to 8 turns for complex cases. We'll provide a sample distribution.
[02:22] Alex Morgan: Perfect. For the bench-harness we usually accept Locust/JMeter/k6 scripts or our own Python harness. Do you have a preference?
[02:34] Ella Rodriguez: Our infra team has existing Locust scripts; we can try to port them if needed. We also have a Python harness that uses asyncio streaming.
[02:45] Priya Nair: Locust is easiest — we have example locustfiles that plug into bench-harness. For streaming tests we use a separate runner that measures per-token latency and backpressure behavior. We'll send both examples.
[03:05] Sophie Wang: When you say streaming runner, does that assume HTTP/2 or a websocket? We currently use SSE for streaming in prod.
[03:17] Priya Nair: We support several streaming transports; SSE is fine. The runner will open persistent connections and measure token arrival timing. There can be noise from client-side buffering, so we usually run a client-side and server-side measurement to correlate.
[03:35] Marcus Lee: On the infra side, we'll either run tests against Redwood-hosted endpoints or inside our VPC for private pilot. What credentials and networking do you need?
[03:47] Alex Morgan: For Redwood-hosted we just need API key and a stable URL we'll provide. For VPC/private runs we'll need a temporary test endpoint and maybe an SSH jumpbox or peered network; we'll provide an integration checklist. We'll include the security pack in the follow-up.
[04:05] Ella Rodriguez: Great. Also curious about measurement of cost — do you report token breakdown and per-route cost during runs?
[04:15] Priya Nair: Yes, our console gives token-level cost, plus per-route latency breakdowns. For the POC we'll export CSVs with token counts, GPU utilization, and per-request timings.
[04:30] Alex Morgan: Ok let's talk dataset — we ask for ~1k representative prompts and 50 longer context examples to stress memory/kv. Ella, you said you'd provide that?
[04:43] Ella Rodriguez: Yes, we'll anonymize and deliver by Monday, and include labels for expected safe outputs and a few regression prompts.
[04:51] Priya Nair: Awesome. On the harness side, we need: locustfile or script, prompt set, expected latency targets, and a short runbook for session emulation. We'll try to avoid custom code if we can wrap your locustfile.
[05:10] [00:05:10] Sophie Wang: Can the harness simulate variable batch sizes and dynamic batching behavior? Our runtime sometimes aggregates small requests into micro-batches.
[05:24] Priya Nair: Yes — bench-harness supports concurrency knobs, and we can adjust client concurrency to influence batching. We also instrument server-side batch histograms. We'll expose batch size distribution in the runs.
[05:40] Marcus Lee: Ok re security — we need to confirm encryption at rest and KMS usage for any artifacts. How do you handle logs and audit trails during POCs?
[05:52] Alex Morgan: We provide audit logs and can integrate with a customer KMS for Private deployments. For hosted POCs, logs are retained short-term and we can sign an NDA for data handling. We'll attach SOC2 summary and the security pack after the call.
[06:10] Ella Rodriguez: Good. On timelines — what's realistic for the benchmark run? We want at least two full steady-state windows to validate.
[06:22] Priya Nair: Typically a 48-72 hour window gives good confidence, but for the POC we can do a focused 2-week engagement with 2-3 dedicated 2hr peak runs and longer soak runs overnight. For acceptance criteria we usually require one steady 2hr run that meets success metrics plus a soak.
[06:40] Alex Morgan: Proposed timeline: Monday deliverables (prompt set + locust file), Tuesday-Thursday integration & smoke runs, run on 2025-10-01 for main load window, and then analysis the week after. Does that align?
[06:55] Ella Rodriguez: Yes that works.
[07:00] Soph ie Wang: (interruption) sorry typo on my end.
[07:05] [00:07:05] Marcus Lee: For private runs, we may need VPC peering; how long does that typically take?
[07:12] Priya Nair: It depends on your security review but we've done peering within 1-3 business days when customers provide the necessary CIDR and contact info. If that's too slow, we can run hosted endpoints first.
[07:25] Ella Rodriguez: We'll try hosted first to move faster. If results look good we'll open the peering path.
[07:32] Alex Morgan: About metrics — we'll collect p50/p95/p99 latencies, per-token latency for streaming, throughput curves, batch size histograms, GPU utilization, and token counts. We will also run quality checks with your labeled prompts to catch any regressions.
[07:50] Priya Nair: For quality we can run an automated eval on the responses and report BLEU/ROUGE or simple exact-match metrics for deterministic prompts. For open-ended LLM outputs we'll use scoring harness you already have or manual spot checks.
[08:05] Ella Rodriguez: For some subcomponents we need determinism — we'll mark a small subset of prompts as golden and expect perfect or near-perfect outputs under the POC.
[08:14] Alex Morgan: Understood. We'll flag those in the bench results.
[08:20] [00:08:20] Priya Nair: A couple of practical notes: 1) if your Locust script uses custom client libs we might need to stub or containerize them; 2) streaming tests require clock-synchronized clients to measure true per-token latencies; 3) please avoid very bursty traffic during initial smoke runs.
[08:45] Marcus Lee: We'll containerize the scripts. We'll also try to provide a small staging cluster for initial tests.
[08:53] Sophie Wang: Any gotchas around quantized models or smaller instance types? We might want to see 8-bit quantized runs to hit cost targets.
[09:03] Priya Nair: We can run quantized variants. The bench-harness reports quality delta and throughput change. Quantization sometimes introduces slight latency reductions per token but can affect quality slightly; we'll include quality regression checks.
[09:20] Ella Rodriguez: For running the actual load, do you recommend streaming or non-streaming baseline first?
[09:28] Priya Nair: Start with non-streaming so we get stable p95 numbers; then move to streaming runner to measure per-token behavior. They exercise different paths in the runtime.
[09:38] Alex Morgan: Also good to capture backend metrics: GPU GPU stall, memory pressure, and RPC queue length. We'll gather that in our exported CSVs.
[09:50] [00:09:50] Marcus Lee: Great. Anything else on tooling? You mentioned bench-harness repo — can you outline files we should expect?
[09:59] Priya Nair: Repo contains: example locustfile, python streaming runner, a wrapper to push results to S3, and a post-processing notebook. We'll also include a template for expected-results JSON to declare golden prompts.
[10:15] Ella Rodriguez: Perfect. Sophie: are you okay with the proposed timeline?
[10:20] Sophie Wang: Yes, as long as we can get the prompt set and credentials quick.
[10:25] Alex Morgan: We'll follow up after the call with the repo link, example scripts, and the security pack. Priya will own the integration work.
[10:34] Priya Nair: I'll add a few notes — for streaming we may ask you to run a short local client to validate SSE latency before the main run; this reduces unknowns. Also, if you want to stress test fallback behavior we can configure model-variant fallbacks in the routing so we can simulate outages.
[10:55] [00:10:55] Ella Rodriguez: We also want to check cost projection for sustained loads. Can you provide a sample cost run?
[11:03] Alex Morgan: Yes we'll provide a cost sample per 1M tokens under the config used in the run, plus a quick sensitivity table for batching vs concurrency.
[11:15] Marcus Lee: A small request — can the harness produce per-request IDs so we can correlate with our logs?
[11:23] Priya Nair: Yep we'll include request_id in the payload and in the exported CSV.
[11:30] [00:11:30] Sophie Wang: One last thing on acceptance: we'll accept the POC if the main run meets p95 < 300ms non-streaming, streaming per-token < 30ms median, no quality regressions on golden set, and token cost within 20% of your pilot estimate.
[11:50] Alex Morgan: That's a clear acceptance criteria — we'll sign up to that and capture it in the SOW.
[12:00] [00:12:00] Ella Rodriguez: Great. So to recap, Priya shares repo and scripts by tomorrow, Cloudline shares prompts and locustfile early next week, and main run target 2025-10-01.
[12:12] Alex Morgan: Correct. We'll also send the security doc and pilot SOW draft. Any blockers?
[12:20] Marcus Lee: No blockers on our side but need to loop in security for any peering.
[12:28] Sophie Wang: We'll review the SOW and confirm.
[12:35] Alex Morgan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with links and a calendar invite for the run.
[12:42] [00:12:42] Meeting end
